prime.problem: There are a dozen ways to get structured output: prompt and repair, JSON mode, provider strict modes, Ollama, vLLM with three backends, and more. Choosing by popularity or by one benchmark number picks a tool whose failure mode you didn't plan for: a schema the API rejects, a compile on every request, or a keyword quietly ignored.
prime.fits: The capstone decision card. Every row cites a number from an earlier card: parse rates (why JSON breaks), coverage (coverage and compliance), compile time (compile vs per-token), recursion (grammars), reasoning fields (quality). Use it once you can explain those, and come back to it when you have a real decision.
expect: four questions: who reads it, logits access, schema fixed or dynamic, hard features
prime.goal: Walk any real use case through the four questions to a route, justify it with one number per question, and name the test you'd run before committing.

attend: Why is "who reads the output?" the first question, before any engine comparison?
Which single question separates XGrammar from llguidance, and what number decides it?
Why does question 4 (hard features) sit under every self-hosted route instead of in one branch?
In the "what each route delivers" table, which column never reaches 30/30 without code, and why?
When does the guide say prompt-only is the right answer despite everything else in the course?

must: A machine consumer can't tolerate a parse failure → constrain decoding (7/30 → 30/30 raw) → a person reading loosely can live with prompt + light cleaning (29/30 schema-valid after cleaning)

Only whoever runs the model can mask → a closed model means its strict mode and its schema subset (compliance 0.92–1.00 when accepted, declared coverage falling to 0.06) → self-hosting gives you the backend choice

Schema fixed and reused → compile once, amortise (XGrammar precomputes; 0.11–0.30 s alongside prefill) → schema new per request → pick near-zero compile (llguidance 0.00–0.02 s vs Outlines 3.06–12.77 s)
Hard features (recursion, oneOf, counts, patterns) → engines differ in what they accept and enforce → test your real schemas with a validator before committing, because declared ≠ enforced
elevated: No route fixes values → the constrained route is 30/30 valid but 22/30 correct until the total is computed in code → every path in the tree ends with a value check
reference: engine and backend names per route (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, MAX, MLC-LLM)
the JSON-mode check details (10 runs, 7 key sets)

compress.prompt: Close the card and draw the four-question tree from memory, with each leaf's route and one number that justifies it. Then write the one step that follows every leaf.
checklist: 1. who reads it: machine → constrain; person → prompt + light cleaning
2. logits: API → provider strict mode within its subset; self-host → choose a backend
3. schema: fixed → XGrammar-style precompute; dynamic → llguidance-style on-the-fly
4. hard features: test coverage on your own schemas first
fallback: schema rejected → prompt + repair loop
after every leaf: validate values in code

retrieve.q: Explain why the guide is a path of questions rather than a single formula, and what the whole-picture formula can't tell you.
answer: the formula compares cost and pass rate among candidates you already have
some constraints rule candidates out entirely: no logits access, a schema outside an API's subset, recursion an FSM can't do
those are yes/no gates, so they come first as questions

retrieve.q: Walk this case through the four questions: a support tool builds a JSON Schema from each customer's form definition and needs a validated object for a database, on a self-hosted open model.
answer: 3. a new schema per request: near-zero compile, so llguidance (GCT 0.00–0.02 s)
4. forms may use patterns or oneOf: run their real schemas through the engine with a validator; then check values in code

retrieve.q: A teammate wants to standardise on one route for every team. Which route comes closest, and what does standardising cost?
answer: no route wins every question: closed models force strict mode, dynamic schemas punish precompute, recursion rules out FSM backends
the closest general default is a grammar engine with low compile time plus a validator, with prompt + repair as the fallback
the cost: some teams give up their best model or their fastest option, so standardise the checks, not the engine

compare.q: The whole-picture card gives a cost formula; this card gives a decision tree. When would following the formula alone lead you to the wrong tool, and when would the tree alone?
answer: the formula alone: it could pick the fastest engine even though it doesn't cover your schema (coverage isn't in the formula's inputs)
the tree alone: it picks a route without pricing it; two valid routes can differ 10× in time per usable object
use the tree to narrow the candidates, then the formula to price them

compare.q: Where it runs maps the stack; this card picks a route through it. Which question in the tree is really a question about the stack, and what does the stack add that the tree doesn't show?
answer: question 2 (can you reach the logits?) is a stack question: who runs the sampling loop
the stack adds scale: Ollama for one user, vLLM/SGLang for batching, and per-request grammar state
and the provider-specific keyword limits that decide question 4 on hosted APIs

predict.q: A schema is static, used a million times, self-hosted, and recursive (a comment tree). The tree's question 3 says "XGrammar". Is anything about the recursion a problem for that choice, and which engine from the course would be ruled out? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: XGrammar is fine: it compiles a CFG to a pushdown automaton and handles recursion, precomputing the stack-independent tokens. What recursion rules out is Outlines-core, which has no PDA. The real risk is the model nesting without end, so set max_tokens or bound the depth in the schema, as the grammars card showed. Then run question 4's test: check that the recursive $ref is accepted and enforced.

apply.task: Write a one-page decision record for a structured-output feature you're building (or: extracting invoices from emails into a database with a self-hosted model; the invoice schema is fixed but has nested line items and an optional oneOf for tax). Answer the four questions with one number or fact each from the course, name the route, name the fallback, and list the three tests you'll run before committing.
apply.done: The record has four answered questions, each citing a card, a route and a fallback, and three concrete tests: a coverage test on real schemas, a value check, and a timing check on a new schema.
apply.hint: Tests from the course: send your real schemas and keep any rejection (coverage); probe with deliberately invalid instances (over/under); validate values in code and count errors separately (valid is not correct); time a fresh schema end to end on your own engine (compile vs per-token).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether recursion rules out XGrammar?
Which of the four questions could you not answer with a number from the course?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: schema reuse → backend choice, or declared features → enforced features?
